highlights:
# Someone on your team sees 1,979 TFLOPS BF16 on the H100 spec sheet and plans capacity around it. A few weeks in, the bill does not match that number. | Spheron Network · LinkedIn · 2026-09-15T00:00:00+00:00

...

Someone on your team sees 1,979 TFLOPS BF16 on the H100 spec sheet and plans capacity around it. A few weeks in, the bill does not match that number.

TFLOPS is a chip's raw math speed. It is measured in trillions of operations per second. The 1,979 figure assumes 2:4 sparsity. That's a trick that skips half the values in a calculation to run faster. Most real workloads never use that trick, so you never see that speed.

An H100 runs on-demand at $2.65 an hour no matter what you do with it. What changes is how much of that hour the chip is actually busy doing work.

Prefill is the phase where the model reads your prompt. It keeps the GPU close to fully busy. Decode is the phase where the model writes the answer one token at a time. It leaves the GPU waiting on memory more than it computes.

- Prefill at 92% utilization: you are effectively paying about $2.88 for every hour of real work
- Decode at 30% utilization: that same $2.65 hour is effectively costing you about $8.83 per hour of real work

The chip and the listed price do not change. The bill does, depending on which phase your traffic sits in most.

The H100's biggest lead is on FP8 work, and the A100 has no FP8 support or Transformer Engine. On Beam, an H100 PCIe machine costs $1.83/hr against $1.36/hr for the A100 80GB SXM4, about 35% more, so the H100 only wins per job if it runs more than 1.35 times faster. results.title: The same GPU, at very different prices · infratoapp
highlights:
The median gap between the cheapest and dearest seller of an identical card is 3.8×. The widest is the V100-16GB: $0.24 per GPU-hour at Verda (DataCrunch) against $2.85 at Runcrate, a gap of 11.8×. An H100 SXM 80GB — the card most of this market is actually built on — runs from $2.16 to $6.16 across 13 sellers, a gap of 2.8×.

These are headline on-demand rates, before any commitment discount, for the same part. Not a similar part, not a different memory configuration, and not one region against another.

### We tell you about a price increase before it takes effect

You say to your agent

> “Is the price of an H100 going to change soon?”

A price increase now always comes at least 24 hours before it takes effect, and we tell you about it. An increase is a higher list price, or a smaller Friday, weekend, or batch job discount.

When we schedule an increase, the dashboard shows a notice until a few days after it takes effect. The admins and billing members of each organization that used that type in the last 90 days get an email.

1. 07:00 UTC

### The H100 price is now $5.04 per GPU-hour

On October 8 at 00:00 Pacific time, the H100 list price changed from $3.96 to $5.04 per GPU-hour. Per GPU-minute, the price changed from $0.066 to $0.084. A whole 8-GPU node now costs $40.32 per hour.

The new price applies to each minute that we bill from that time. This includes the minutes of nodes and jobs that were already running. Minutes before that time bill at the old price.

The discounts did not change, and they now apply to the new list price. Friday hours are 33% off, and Saturday and Sunday hours are 20% off, on the Pacific calendar. Batch jobs are 25% off the list price. The docs show the rates.

We did not tell you about this change before it took effect. We are sorry for the late notice. If you have a question about your bill, send it to us on the contact page.

results.title: An inference cluster running four H100s at full tilt costs $10.28 an hour. The same traffic served through a mixed setup costs $4.01 an hour, with the same tokens going out the … | Spheron Network
results.author: Spheron Network
highlights:
# An inference cluster running four H100s at full tilt costs $10.28 an hour. The same traffic served through a mixed setup costs $4.01 an hour, with the same tokens going out the … | Spheron Network · LinkedIn · 2026-09-30T00:00:00+00:00

**Spheron Network**.

---

An inference cluster running four H100s at full tilt costs $10.28 an hour. The same traffic served through a mixed setup costs $4.01 an hour, with the same tokens going out the door.

Every request has two stages. Prefill reads your prompt and builds the first output token. Decode generates every token after that, one at a time. On a 512-token response, decode eats about 80% of the wall clock.

Decode is memory-bound, not compute-bound. The GPU spends most of its time moving data rather than doing math, so a cheaper card barely loses ground there.

Split the work by stage:
- Prefill runs on the H100, where raw compute reads the prompt fast
- Decode runs on the L40S, which serves tokens for far less per hour

The full numbers: 4x H100 runs $10.28/hr at $0.89 per million tokens. A mixed cluster of 1x H100 plus 2x L40S runs $4.01/hr at $0.46 per million tokens. That is a 61% cut in hourly spend and about 48% cut in cost per token.

We wrote up the setup: vLLM 0.8+ with NVIDIA Dynamo 1.0 routing requests between the two chip types.

results.title: B200 on-demand costs $6.03 an hour. H100 FP8 spot costs $0.99, a fraction of that price. On sticker price alone, H100 looks like the deal. It still does once you account for … | Spheron Network
results.author: Spheron Network
highlights:
B200 on-demand costs $6.03 an hour. H100 FP8 spot costs $0.99, a fraction of that price. On sticker price alone, H100 looks like the deal. It still does once you account for throughput.

The hourly rate ignores how much work each GPU finishes in that hour. FP8 and FP4 are number formats a GPU computes in. FP4 uses fewer bits per number than FP8, so it moves less data and processes more tokens per second.

MLPerf is an independent benchmark, not a Spheron-run test, and its numbers are the best available proxy for real throughput. On MLPerf v4.1, H100 FP8 spot produces 24,525 tokens per second. On MLPerf v5.1, B200 FP4 produces 102,725, about 4.2 times more.
